questions.explanation: The constant 50 multiplies through, and the argument u = 1 + t/50 has rate u' = 1/50, so s'(t) = 50·(1/50)/u = 1/u = 1/(1 + t/50). At t = 50 that is 1/2 = 0.5 meters per unit time, still positive, so the distance is rising but more slowly than at t = 0, where the rate was 1. Nothing in the model turns over; the rate simply shrinks as the log's argument grows.

questions.explanation: The log rule is (ln x)' = 1/x, and it applies to the natural logarithm; a log of another base is a constant multiple, so its derivative carries a factor such as 1/ln 10. The 1/x shape is the base case only when the argument is the variable itself, and when the argument is a function its rate must multiply in. Treating a log as a power, or its inverse e^x as interchangeable, confuses two different rule families.
questions.hint: Ask what the derivative of a power is, then compare.

questions.explanation: The log's argument is a product of two functions of t, so its rate is a'·b + a·b', and the product rule supplies that rate before the log rule divides by the argument. The log law ln(ab) = ln a + ln b is a convenience when the factors are constants, not a replacement for the chain rule. Differentiating as though the argument were the bare t would give 1/(a·b) and lose every rate term.
questions.hint: Differentiate the inside product first, then divide by it.

questions.explanation: With p = ln(x), p' = 1/x. With q = ln(2x), the argument's rate is 2, so q' = 2/(2x) = 1/x. The constant inside the log cancels, so the two models share a slope at every positive x even though q sits ln 2 higher at every point. A bigger argument does not make a log rise faster, which is the whole point of the decaying rate 1/x.
questions.hint: Differentiate both, then simplify each fraction.
